translations.text: A discourse by Father Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, which he delivered about the Canaanite woman.
The storm is great, but it could not hold back the eagerness of those who came.
The trials are many, but they have not undone your hard work.
The church will never cease to be attacked, and it is always victorious.
They plot against it, but it cuts them down.
The more they plan evil against it, the more it grows.
The waves break against one another.
But this rock stands immovable. The word of God is immovable.
He is the one who said, “The gates of Hades will not prevail against it.”
The one who wages war destroys himself, while strengthening the church all the more.
Job was a good man before his trial. But the days when his body was healthy were not like the days when his disease wove a crown and placed it on his head.
Never be afraid of a trial if your soul is prepared.
For just as the furnace does not harm gold, so suffering does not harm the person who bears it with strength.
What does the furnace do to gold? It purifies it all the more.
So it is with the person who stands firm under suffering: endurance comes to him and lifts him up.
Luxury weakens the soul, while a trial strengthens the laity.
Consider, then, what the people of today have done: they have been put to shame. And what have our people, in turn, done through their excellence?
Where are those counted among them? They are not even to be seen.
I come out into the marketplace, and I see no one. They are leaves: the wind came and scattered them. They are chaff that has been winnowed away. The wheat remained pure.
Who is fighting against them? It is their own conscience, striking them, that fights against them.
We will set our table again.
Yesterday Paul set his table before us; today it is Matthew.
Yesterday it was the tentmaker; today it is the tax collector.
Yesterday it was the blasphemer; today it is the obedient man.
Yesterday it was the persecutor; today it is the generous giver.
But the thief did not remain a thief; instead, he became an apostle.
And the plunderer did not remain a robber; instead, he became an evangelist.
I will tell of the wickedness first, and afterward of the virtue.
Your teachers did not shine forth from sin at first, but they shone in righteousness in the end.
For the tax collectors and thieves were the thorns of the earth.
What, then, is a tax collector’s office?
It is a place where people plunder in broad daylight.
Under the law, it is indeed open extortion. It is also extortion that has a law behind it.
He is the spokesman for the robbers.
When a robber is caught stealing, he is ashamed. But this man, the tax collector, is bold as he plunders.
But in an instant he became an evangelist. How? In what way?
As Jesus passed by, he saw him sitting at his tax office. He said to him, “Get up and follow me.”
Oh, the power of the word! The call came, freed the captive, and enlisted him as a soldier.
The call came and turned lead into gold. While he was in the mire of wickedness, it brought him to the summit of virtue.
Let no one give up on his salvation, for evil deeds never possess an inherent nature.
For they too came about through free choice.
Even if you are a tax collector, you can become an evangelist.
Even if you are a robber, you can live in paradise.
Even if you are a magus, you can worship your Lord.
For there is no wickedness that repentance does not remove.
For this reason, God chose the greatest sinners on earth, so that no one would give up on himself.
Do not say, “I have sinned—what will happen?” For you have a physician who provides treatment according to your willingness.
Did he not create you when you did not exist and bring you into existence?
Did he not create you as in the beginning, when he took some earth and shaped it into a human being?
Rather, he made the earth change and become flesh, in the form of sinews, bones, hair, teeth, eyes, the neck, the chest, hands, feet, and all the rest.
Is not the substance of all these things earth?
Craftsmanship came in and fashioned the whole creation in countless forms.
Do not inquire into its form, nor pry into what exists. Instead, believe in the miracle all the more.
Can you explain the manner in which it was made?
If fire comes upon thorns and destroys them,
how much more do the words of God cause sins to dry up and perish!
But even if you say, “I have sinned greatly,”
who, then, is sinless? I confess my sins; you too should confess yours. “Declare your sins first, so that you may be justified.”
If you have sinned, hurry and stand up. Mourn, and let your heart be consumed with remorse. Pour out your tears as well.
For did the sinful woman do anything else besides pouring out her tears? And she received repentance.
Then Jesus came out of the regions of Tyre and Sidon, and behold, a woman rushed toward him.
The evangelist marvels.
“Behold, a woman,” he said, “the devil’s great weapon, the mother of sin, the beginning of lawlessness, the one who cast herself out of paradise. This is her nature; this is woman.”
Oh, these new and wonderful things!
The Jews run away; the woman runs toward him, pleading with him and saying, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Look at this woman who became a preacher, how she acknowledged God’s saving plan. She said, “Lord”—which refers to his divinity—“Son of David”—which refers to his assumption of human nature.
“Have mercy on me, for I have no good deed to my credit, since I belong to this world.”
Look at this wise soul saying, “Have mercy on me!”
“I have no good way of life to my credit, since I belong to this earthly life.”
“I was distressed and ran to the Spirit.”
“Surely you will not question me about my sins?”
“Just grant me salvation. Where the Spirit is, people are not questioned about sins.”
O woman, what did you see? You are a lawless woman and a prostitute.
How did you dare to rush toward him?
Look at this woman’s wisdom.
She did not appeal to the apostles, saying, “Take me in to him.”
She did not beg Peter, nor did she need the others. “I do indeed need them,
but I do not need anyone to bring him into my presence.
Why? Because he came down and took on flesh so that people could speak with him in the flesh.
Oh, this great love of God for humanity!
The one before whom the cherubim tremble in heaven—a sinful woman will stand and speak with him on earth!
“Have mercy on me,” she said. “This is why you took on flesh and set out and came into the world: for a sinner like me.”
They tremble before him in heaven; on earth they speak freely with him.
“Have mercy on me.” “What do you want?”
“I am seeking mercy.”
“What do you want?”
“My daughter is terribly mad. This grief is unbearable.
Save my inward parts, for they are burning me. My insides are suffering. Care for me in this burning heat.
What shall I do? I am going to die.”
Why did she not say, “Have mercy on my daughter”?
Instead, she said, “Have mercy on me. My daughter does not feel the pain of the illness because she is mad.
This great, violent illness surrounds her, because she is unaware of it.
Have mercy on me, for I see this spectacle every day.
My grief is great.
What shall I call her? Shall I call her a corpse? But she moves and is alive, yet she does not know what she is doing.
For I do not know its name so that I might understand the nature of the illness. If my daughter had died,
“For death belongs to everyone.”
how would I be looking at the eyes distorted by her trembling, the hands whose bones have come out of joint, and the hair being torn out in her madness,
and the mouth that pours out foam, while the one fighting against her lurks inside her without showing himself?
Have mercy on me. My storm is fierce.
Such is the nature of that illness of mine, and the terror of the demon. Have mercy on me.”
Look at this woman’s wisdom.
Why did she not go to magicians, or exorcists, or women who cast spells,
or diviners, who honor demons and cause the suffering of the sick to increase and their pain to grow worse?
Instead, she left the devil’s tribunal behind and came before the Savior of souls: “Have mercy on me! My daughter is severely afflicted.”
Have you seen her firmness and endurance,
and how this woman stood there? Yet he did not answer her a word.
Oh, these common affairs!
She begs him, cries out, and pleads, but he does not answer her a word.
The sickness increases; the Master remains silent.
The wound is [?] and [?]; the Word remains silent.
The physician holds back his hand.
What is this new and astonishing thing?
You run after others, saying, “Come to me, and I will heal you.”
But she, for her part, runs after you, and you run away from her.
“Have mercy on me!” “I was not sent to anyone—to anyone except the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
His disciples approached him and begged him, saying, “Send her away, because she is crying out behind us.”
You yourself see her outward cry; the cry of her heart is also great before you.
And again they spoke to him as Lord and lover of humanity: “Save this woman.”
“What am I to do? I was not sent to anyone except the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
This, then, is the whole matter.
Was this, then, why you took on flesh, so that you would pass by a woman who is about to perish?
Will you then leave the inhabited world deserted—the Scythians, the Arabs, the Elamites, Cilicia, Cappadocia, the Syrians, the people of Phoenicia, and every place on which the sun shines?
Did you come here, then, only for the Jews,
and leave the Gentiles themselves deserted?
Will you then remain indifferent while they insult your Father and worship idols?
How does David say according to the flesh, “Ask me, and I will give you nations as your inheritance, and your dominion will reach to the ends of the earth”?
Likewise Isaiah, who saw the seraphim, says, “The root of Jesse will appear, and the one who rises to rule the nations; the nations will put their hope in him.”
And again, “A ruler will not disappear from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things reserved for him come; and he is the one the nations await.”
And again, “All you nations, clap your hands!”
You too, O lover of every soul, are the one who said to your disciples, “Go and baptize all the nations in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.”
Since this woman was a Canaanite, she caught the good fragrance.
She came out of the place of madness and bewilderment, the place where idols are worshiped.
This poor woman came, pleading about what had afflicted her daughter. And you said, “I was not sent to anyone except the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
Yet when the centurion came to you, you said, “I will come and heal him.”
And again, in the case of the robber, you said to him, “Today you will be with me in my paradise.”
And again, the paralyzed man whom you told to pick up his bed walked.
And again, Lazarus, whom you called—it was his fourth day in the tomb.
You raise the dead; you bind up those who have come apart.
You make prostitutes more self-controlled than virgins.
Why, then, did you not answer this poor Canaanite woman?
He said, “[?] take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
Oh, the care of this physician! He knows that she gives off a fragrance.
But all these words serve to shame the Jews, because they are called children.
They have taken on the nature of dogs.
As Paul said, “Beware of the dogs.”
“Beware of the evil workers. Beware of the mutilation.”
And again she said, “Have mercy on me.”
But he said, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
“Yes, Lord, you call me a dog; I acknowledge it. You treat me like a dog.”
“Lord, give to me as to a dog. I do not refuse a crumb.”
You too, give me some of what belongs to you.
You call me a dog; give me some crumbs.
For even dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.
What did he say to her—the one who had refused her until now, who had driven her away and cast her out?
“Woman!” Immediately she received praise.
God says, “Woman!” Let those who pray listen when I say, “Appeal to God and plead with him.”
And you yourself say, “I appealed to him once, and I prayed twice and three times, and ten and twenty times I bent my knees.”
You did bend your knees, and your mouth speaks, but your heart calculates interest. You are thinking about your companions and your possessions.
Your soul stands at the door. Do not withdraw until you receive what you ask for.
For it happens with some people that, when they go to church, they recite tens of thousands of lines of words.
For God does not need many words. He needs only your prayer, for you to imitate this Canaanite woman.
Pray wherever you are.
Even if you are in the bathhouse or on the road, pray.
Even if you are brought before a judge, pray.
Has the judge sent for you? Let your prayer go ahead of you to God. He is not looking for a place; rather, God is looking for a good disposition.
While Jeremiah was in the muddy pit, he found God there and prayed to him.
While Daniel was in the lions’ den, God helped him.
While the three holy men were in the furnace, they found God and pleaded with him.
While Job was on the dung heap among the worms, he found God and called upon him.
You too, if you call upon him, he will listen to you in your prayer.
Imitate this Canaanite woman.
For if you enter the church among the Persians, the Goths, the Indians, or the Moors, you will hear Christ crying out, “Woman, great is your faith!”
And look, a long time has passed since she gave praise, and the honor of her memory endures and flourishes.
Even if you do not have a daughter who is possessed by a demon, you do have your soul, which is sinning.
He has pity on the person possessed by a demon, but he hates the person who sins.
A demon-possessed person is not held accountable, but someone who sins has no defense.
When did the Canaanite woman cast out the demon?
At the moment when Christ said to her, “Woman, great is your faith!”
The Son of God was casting out demons. For is he a human being who must go to the place where the demon is? Rather, he is God, filling every place.
If someone wants to go to a ruler on some occasion,
let his attendant answer you.
Otherwise, he will tell you, “He is not available,” or, “He is asleep.”
But God is not like this. Whenever you call to him, he will listen to you, at any time.
No eunuch prevents you, nor any steward.
You too should say, “Have mercy on me,” like this Canaanite woman, and he will come to you immediately.
Look at this expression: it reveals the Son of God as being like his Father, comparing him to him.
Now, when God created heaven, he said, “Let there be a heaven,” and it came into being.
And, “Let there be an earth,” and it came into being.
“Let there be air,” and it came into being.
“Let the sun and the moon come into being,” and they came into being.
Oh, the goodness of God! He makes known to us the Son, who is equal to the good Father in everything, in divinity.
The Father said in the Old Testament, “Let them come into being,” and they came into being.
The Son likewise said, “Let it happen for you as you wish,” and it happened. Her daughter was healed from that very moment.
What, then? The Canaanite woman cast the demon out of her daughter, and she also cast out her own, according to the command of the Savior of souls.
Through the mercy and compassion of our God and his grace, our own are also healed.
For all these things, let us give thanks to God the Father and to the Son, Christ Jesus, who taught us through his Holy Spirit, “I am in my Father, and my Father is in me.”

To him belongs glory forever and ever. Amen.

Eusebius, bishop.
Likewise, an exposition by Apa John, Archbishop of Constantinople, concerning the blessed Susanna.
We have come to you again with great goodwill.
We are the ones who owe you a discourse,
not to fulfill our obligation as we ought,
but to give what we owe according to what we have.
[?] His hand is indeed open to our eagerness, and he stretches it out to give more than we can offer.
But the poverty of our words is severely limiting.
Therefore we will ask you to accept small things, if not great ones.
But if someone accepts small things and enlarges them through the eagerness of his heart, then we will not be lacking.
Your eagerness will make up for the part in which we are lacking.
For both the meager offerings of the poor and the abundant offerings of the rich—
when God sees them, he accepts them with equal honor.
Or perhaps he will honor the offerings of the poor more, because he looks at the heart’s eagerness, not at the abundance of wealth.
Let the account of the poor widow who threw two small coins into the treasury serve as proof of this for you.
For the honor of her offering became greater in the Lord’s eyes than that of the gold the rich brought in.
For God did not need gold, but a pure heart and a will directed toward what is good.
So now we too open our hearts in purity,
and bring in the word of God, present it well, and deposit it in the treasuries of your souls, so that we may give you what we can.
For I remember that yesterday I promised you that I would proclaim the strength of Susanna’s chastity,
so that these things might benefit many, just as Joseph’s struggle in his chastity and his battle benefited many.
So now let Susanna too compete in the arena filled with crowds.
Let her compete where God and the angels, as well as men and women, watch her, so that she may teach young girls to scorn death for the sake of chastity.
Susanna, this pearl, was noble by birth and beautiful in appearance.
She had remained secluded in her bedroom from childhood, having grown up in a dignified way of life. But when Satan turned his attention to her youth,
she committed herself to the bond of marriage according to the law.
She guarded her husband’s marriage bed and the rightful bond of her marriage without violating it.
Her eyes never wandered about, looking for an unfamiliar young man.
Nor did she ever let her ears listen to the melodies of filthy songs.
Nor did she let her nostrils delight in the fragrance of clothes perfumed with incense.
In short, she did not allow any of her senses to run wild, lest the chastity guarded in her heart be destroyed and her soul slide down into a fleeting pleasure through the defilements of deception.
For most sins arise in the soul through the senses.
For the soul lives in the heart like a virgin resting quietly in her bedroom, with the five senses serving as her servants.
The senses are the eye—that is, sight—hearing, smell, taste, and touch. So if none of the senses goes astray or becomes corrupted,
the soul remains quietly by herself, safe from harm.
But if the eye turns toward a young boy and the wave of desire surges upward, the storm of pleasure immediately strikes her.
It separates her from purity, and she goes and becomes entangled in sin. She enters the flood into which David entered,
about which he then cried out, saying, “I have come into the depths of the sea; a storm has submerged me.”
Likewise, if hearing takes in a sweet voice and the deception of those filthy songs, and the heart turns toward them, they drag it down into their ruin.
Again, if taste gives itself over to abundant food and much wine, it drags the soul down into confusion and stumbling.
But smell, too, if it delights in the pleasant fragrance of ointments and perfumes, falls into deception.
And it binds the soul together with itself in that deception.
So if the pure soul becomes involved in these things, she becomes like a virgin betrayed by her own servants,
who has slipped down into sin and lack of self-control.
For when lack of self-control creeps into the soul, it behaves like a thief.
It enters the storerooms of the heart, makes it desolate, and leaves it stripped of purity.
Now this blessed woman, Susanna, had guarded her eyes, her hands, her feet, her tongue, her eyelids, and the whole condition of her senses.
And she truly was, according to the saying of the wise man, like a locked garden and a sealed spring, so that no one could plunder her
and destroy the dwelling place of perfumes and purity, and draw water out of that place beside the spring of self-control.
The two elders lusted after this woman—those who were thought to guide the people.
They were burning with their desire.
They were ashamed to tell one another about the fire blazing in their hearts.
One day, each of them went secretly to watch Susanna.
They encountered one another, and when they questioned each other, they confessed the matter to one another.
Then they agreed together to carry out the sinful act and to share in the wickedness.
They were watching for a time when they would find her alone.
One day Susanna went into her husband’s garden to bathe there, as was her custom during the heat of the day.
And she sent her servants out to bring her washing soda and soap.
The elders suddenly rushed at her like wolves attacking a lamb.
They seized her, wanting to carry out their filthy desire with her.
Susanna was between the two elders, who were more wicked than the lions among which Daniel had been.
There was no servant beside her, no neighbor, no acquaintance, and no young girl. There was no one to help her from any direction except God alone, who was watching over her from heaven.
God could indeed have stopped them.
But he allowed them to proceed so that the contest would take place and their hidden intentions would be exposed.
For Susanna’s chastity would expose the elders’ lack of self-control.
And in this way women would find a good source of instruction through Susanna’s firmness.
So a great battle and a great contest lay ahead.
And Susanna faced a harder ordeal than Joseph.
For Joseph was a man struggling against just one woman.
But she was a woman struggling against two men who were forceful in their actions.
And the remarkable thing is that she was struggling against them in a garden, [?] where the serpent had succeeded in deceiving Eve.
This spectacle was great and pleasing. It was great because those fighting in this contest were elders who claimed to be leaders of the people.
It was also pleasing because of the chastity of a weak woman who had the strength to resist these leaders. Then, when they prepared to fight all at once,
the heavens opened and the trumpets sounded.
The contest was ready, and the true judge of the contest was watching from heaven. The multitude of angels was watching from on high.
The serpent was at work in these lawless elders, while faith was showing its strength in this chaste woman.
And there was great anxiety on both sides at once.
The elders were anxious that a woman might defeat them.
Susanna, for her part, was anxious that she might lose her chastity.
And the demons were preparing the wages for these lawless men.
The angels, for their part, were preparing honors for Susanna from heaven.
And these lawless men seized her.
They challenged her with their opening words, saying, “We are the elders of the people.
We have been entrusted with the law and the authority to loose and bind in every matter.
There is no one here who can see us.
So obey us and be with us.
For we desire you. If you do not comply with us, we will testify falsely against you, saying that a young man was with you,
and that this is why you sent a servant away.”
See, then, how many terrible things surrounded this lone woman, Susanna:
deception, a defiling act,
a threat announcing death to her,
condemnation that would make all the people ridicule her,
hatred that would make her husband and her relatives hate her,
grief for her neighbors and the members of her household,
in short, the utter destruction of her entire household.
But none of these schemes could overcome this chaste woman.
For her hope and her heart were firmly set on the God of heaven.
Susanna sighed deeply
and said, “I am hemmed in on every side.
For if I do this, I will die.
But if I do not do it, I will not escape your hands.
Nevertheless, it is better for me not to do this and to fall into your hands than to sin before the Lord.
Woe to me! My shepherds, whom I think of as caring for me—
I see them acting as wolves around me.
The harbors I have in mind, where the ship of my soul was moored—
these I have found sinking me more than a violent storm.
So do not think that I will be afraid of you and obey you and defile my chastity.”
I will not bring shame on my parents.
I will not disgrace my noble birth.
I will not cause my husband grief.
I will not undo the bond of my marriage, by which I am bound to him.
I will not listen to your foolish words.
I will choose to die a violent death rather than lie in a defiled bed.
My husband is with me, even if not in body, but in the desire of my heart.
And my parents’ faces are before me at all times.
So you too should fear God, who sees us.
Be ashamed before the angels who are with us night and day.
Recognize who you are.
Understand the law that you read.
For the law cries out, “You must not desire to have sexual relations with your neighbor.”
And when she had said these things, she cried out, wanting witnesses to come and testify to their misconduct.
The elders also cried out.
And look, Susanna’s servants and her young daughters ran in and saw the elders quarreling with her.
And when the elders spoke their words,
the servants were deeply ashamed, because they had never heard anything like this said against Susanna.
The next day, a great crowd gathered.
For the battle still lay before the victory, and the trial lay before the crown.
All the people gathered together: men, women, and little children.
The audience became very large.
The people below did not understand what they were seeing [?].
But those in heaven understood everything.
And the elders came, full of lawlessness.
And they summoned Susanna, as those who were plotting against her intended. Did they summon her to shame and death, as the judge intended for her, or did they summon her to life and glory forever?
Then they said before the people, “Send for Susanna, the daughter of Hilkiah.”
So they sent for her, and she came with her parents, all her relatives, and her children.
Susanna came as someone deserving death because of her great foolishness.
And she was groaning and grieving, not because she was going to die,
But because she would leave her parents with a bad name and bring disgrace upon her entire family.
For she had no witness there concerning the deed they had accused her of in the garden.
Many were sighing over her: her parents, her friends, her relatives, and her neighbors.
Her husband and his entire household were mourning, and they were all ashamed.
She herself was heartbroken and downcast, weeping and trembling, in deep humiliation.
She came and stood in the midst of everyone.
And the whole crowd stood looking at her, angels and humans alike.
The two elders stood up in their disguise as sheep, though they were wolves.
And the deceiving serpent was speaking within them.
They laid their hands on her.
And they said, “Yesterday we were walking alone in the garden.
This woman came in with two female servants.
She sent the servants out and shut the garden gates.
A young man who had been hiding came in to her and slept with her.
When we saw this unlawful act, while we were hidden in a corner of the garden, we ran toward them.
We could not seize him, because he was stronger than we were.
He opened the gates and ran away.
But we seized this woman and asked her, ‘Who is this young man who was with you?’
But she would not tell us.
These are the things we testify to, having seen them.”
The entire assembly believed them because they were elders and judges, and they condemned her to death.
So they were taking Susanna out to kill her, and no one was defending the truth except God alone.
It was he who [?] allowed these things to happen, so that through the two of them the conduct of each might be fully revealed:
the wickedness, lack of self-control, and shamelessness of the lawless men, on the one hand, and Susanna’s steadfastness even to the point of death, on the other.
Do you see how God neglects the faithful?
He leaves them behind to test them, like gold in a furnace, examining the righteous through various trials.
For this is what he did to Abraham.
For he took Isaac to offer him up as a burnt offering.
He built the altar, but the sheep was not there.
He arranged the wood on it, but there was no ram there.
He took the knife in his hands.
And he set his mind on slaughtering Isaac, and immediately
God made him draw back his hand with a voice.
I have [?] these things, then, so that each of us, when tested and brought close to death, will not lose hope in God’s help,
but will wait for it until it comes to him. Finally, then, they were taking Susanna out to put her to death.
And there was no help anywhere around her.
But when she saw that there was no help among human beings,
she ran to the helper in heaven, the trustworthy witness, the eye that never sleeps.
And she said, “Eternal God, you who understand what is hidden in the heart, who know all things before they happen,
you alone know that these men have testified falsely against me.
And look, I am going to die, although I have done none of the things about which these men have testified falsely against me.”
And the one who said, “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Look, I am here,’” heard her.
As they were taking her out to put her to death, God stirred up the Holy Spirit in a young boy named Daniel.
And he cried out in a loud voice, “I am innocent of this woman’s blood!”
Then the people turned toward him.
And they said, “What is this that you are saying?”
You. But he stood in their midst.
And he said, “Are you so foolish, house of Israel? Return to the place of judgment!
For these men have testified falsely against her.” All the people hurried back.
And Daniel said to them, “Separate them from one another so that I can question them.”
And he said to each one of them, “You who have grown old in evil days, now
your sins, which you have committed from the beginning, have come upon you.
Tell me, under what kind of tree did you see them talking with one another?”
He said, “Under a mastic tree.”
Daniel said to him, “You have truly lied against your own head!
For the angel of God now stands with a sword in his hand, about to cut you in half.”
Then he had them set this man aside.
Then he called the other man and said to him, “You offspring of Canaan, not of Judah! Beauty has deceived you, and lust has torn your heart apart.
Tell me, under what kind of tree did you see them talking with one another?”
He said, “Under an oak tree.”
And Daniel said to him, “You too have lied against your own head!
For look, the angel of God stands with his sword in his hand to cut you in half.”
And all the people shouted loudly, saying, “Blessed is the Lord God, who saves everyone who puts their hope in him!”
And innocent blood was saved that day.
And what David said was fulfilled in Susanna: “My soul has clung to you,
and it was your right hand that took hold of me.”
But these lawless elders who sought Susanna’s life—
they will go down into the earth.
They will be handed over to the sword, and [?] will become a portion for the foxes, which are the demons.
But the king will rejoice in God—that is, Susanna.
And everyone who swears by him will be honored—that is, everyone who believes in him.
For the mouths of those who speak unjustly were shut—that is, these lawless elders.
Then the sorrow of Susanna’s parents turned to joy.
And her husband rejoiced and gave glory to God.
And all her relatives rejoiced.
Her neighbors were glad, and her whole household rejoiced.
And, in short, joy came to them before God, the angels, and people.
You have seen the strength of Susanna’s soul.
You have seen the wisdom of this weak vessel.
The virtuous soul endures, firm in immortality.
It endures with flourishing fruit that never withers.
It endures in unfailing virtue, clothed in God’s help.
So this woman was honored by people and exalted by the angels.
And she was crowned by God.
Make yourselves like her, women! Strive to imitate her character,
so that you too may be worthy of the very same honor as hers from God, in Christ Jesus our Lord. Glory to him forever and ever. Amen.
Father John, Archbishop.
